<reason>A more convincingly addressed the proposition’s comparative benefit–harm claim. B offered a plausible mechanism for relief, but repeatedly weighed background suicide risk as though it established treatment benefit, without adequately weighing lasting harms. A answered the evidentiary-standard challenge with feasible longitudinal comparisons and transparent attrition accounting, making B’s continued accusation of demanding impossible certainty unpersuasive. A also maintained the important distinction between low regret and low harm. B’s argument that uncertainty favors access did not establish the superior outcomes asserted by the motion.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A’s strongest rebuttal targeted B’s concession that suicide prevention was only mechanistically plausible: the severity of suicide cannot substitute for assessing how much treatment reduces its probability. This directly undermined B’s central comparison between potentially fatal untreated distress and manageable treatment risks.</best_rebuttal>
